To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a high-content cytotoxic assay that directly measures cell number provides more accurate cytotoxicity data than a homogenous assay that measures mitochondrial activity.

the high-content cytotoxic cell-based assay we have developed is more sensitive to drug effects than the most widely used homogeneous colorimetric assay, and that this high-content assay can be adapted for specific applications, including the quantification of drug-induced changes in tubulin mass in cells.

we have developed a scalable high-content cytotoxcity assay that is insensitive to changes in the mitochondrial metabolic activity and that can be used to simultaneously measure the effects of anticancer drugs on cell proliferation, mitochondrial mass and nuclear morphology.

the development of a high-throughput screening (HCS)-based assay for the quantification of drug-induced cytotoxicity in individual cells.
the development of new methods for high content screening of anticancer agents and the application of these methods to study the mechanisms of drug action.
the discovery and development of novel anticancer agents.

the use of HCS for cell-based assays is highly recommended.

HCS provides a powerful and versatile platform for quantitative assessment of cell proliferation and drug cytotoxicity.

the HCS method can be applied for the discovery and development of new anticancer agents, as well as to monitor the effects of known agents on cell growth and proliferation.
